meta.title: Information & Computation — entropy, computability, complexity
meta.note: Explanations authored for Bucket Academy (original prose; equations, theorems, and standard definitions are facts). Open sources only. Foundations-first DAG spanning information theory (entropy, mutual information, channel capacity, coding, Kolmogorov complexity), computability (Turing machines, Church–Turing, halting, decidability), automata & formal languages (DFA/NFA, the Chomsky hierarchy), complexity (P, NP, NP-completeness, reductions, space), algorithms & data structures (asymptotics, divide & conquer, dynamic programming, graphs), logic (propositional, predicate, proof systems), cryptography basics (one-way functions, public key), and a learning-theory frontier (PAC learning, VC dimension, the link to statistical mechanics, a modern-ML glimpse).

atoms.title: The bit — the unit of information
atoms.summary: One bit is the information in answering a single yes/no question whose two answers are equally likely.

depths.eli5: A bit is one perfect yes-or-no answer. If you had to guess a number from 1 to 8, three good yes/no questions always nail it — that's three bits.
depths.core: Information is measured by how much it reduces uncertainty. The natural unit is the bit: the amount of information gained from learning the outcome of a fair coin flip. Choosing among 2^n equally likely options takes exactly n bits, because each bit halves the field of possibilities.
depths.deep: The bit is dimensionless and logarithmic by necessity: information about independent events must add, while the number of joint outcomes multiplies, and log is the unique function turning products into sums. Using log base 2 fixes the unit as the bit; base e gives nats, base 10 gives dits/hartleys — same quantity, different ruler.

atoms.note: log2(N) bits identify one item out of N equally likely ones. Memorize: 10 bits ≈ a thousand, 20 bits ≈ a million, 30 bits ≈ a billion.
atoms.art_prompt: a branching binary tree where each yes/no fork halves a crowd of candidate outcomes until one remains

quiz.prompt: How many bits of information does learning the outcome of one fair coin flip provide?
quiz.answer: Exactly one bit.

quiz.prompt: You must identify one card from a standard 52-card deck. What is the minimum number of yes/no questions (bits) needed on average if each answer is maximally informative?
quiz.answer: log2(52) ≈ 5.7 bits, so 6 well-chosen yes/no questions suffice.

atoms.title: Probability distribution and expectation
atoms.summary: A distribution assigns nonnegative weights summing to one; expectation is the weighted average of outcomes.

depths.eli5: If different things can happen with different chances, the expectation is what you'd get on average if you ran the whole thing many times.
depths.core: A discrete random variable X takes values x with probabilities p(x) ≥ 0 that sum to 1. The expectation E[X] = Σ x p(x) is the long-run average; expectation is linear: E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y] even when X and Y are dependent. Almost every quantity in information theory is an expectation of some log-probability.
depths.deep: Linearity of expectation is the workhorse of algorithm analysis precisely because it needs no independence — you sum per-element contributions regardless of correlations. Variance, by contrast, does require care about covariance.

atoms.art_prompt: a histogram of outcome bars whose heights are probabilities, with a balance point marked at the mean

quiz.prompt: State the linearity-of-expectation rule and the one condition it does NOT require.
quiz.answer: E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y]; it does not require X and Y to be independent.

quiz.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is E[X]?

atoms.title: Shannon entropy
atoms.summary: Entropy is the average number of bits needed to describe an outcome — the exact amount of uncertainty in a distribution.

depths.eli5: Entropy measures how surprised you'll be on average. A coin that's always heads has zero entropy (no surprise); a fair coin has one bit (maximum surprise for two outcomes).
depths.core: Shannon entropy H(X) = −Σ p(x) log2 p(x) is the expected 'surprise' −log2 p(x), measured in bits. It is the unique measure (up to scale) satisfying continuity, additivity over independent variables, and maximality for the uniform distribution. It sets the absolute floor on lossless compression: you cannot, on average, encode X in fewer than H(X) bits per symbol.
depths.deep: Surprise is −log2 p because rarer events carry more information, independent events' surprises must add (and probabilities multiply), and log is the function that converts the one into the other. Entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution and is zero exactly when one outcome is certain. It is concave in p, which is why mixing distributions never decreases uncertainty.

atoms.note: Joint and conditional entropy obey the chain rule H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X); conditioning never increases entropy: H(X|Y) ≤ H(X).
sources: Shannon, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (1948, facts)
Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (definitions/facts)
atoms.art_prompt: a dial of distributions from a stuck all-heads coin (entropy 0) to a fair coin (entropy 1 bit), with surprise meters beside each

quiz.prompt: Compute the entropy of a biased coin with P(heads)=1/4.
Explain in one or two sentences why entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution.
quiz.answer: Uncertainty is greatest when no outcome is favored, so every outcome equally likely leaves you maximally unable to predict — any imbalance gives a hint that lowers average surprise.

atoms.title: Source coding theorem (and Kraft inequality)
atoms.summary: Lossless codes can compress a source down to its entropy, and no further — entropy is the compression limit.

depths.eli5: You can give short codewords to common things and long ones to rare things, like Morse code does with 'e'. But there's a hard floor: you can't beat the entropy, on average.
depths.core: Shannon's source coding theorem says the minimum expected codeword length for a symbol source equals its entropy: H(X) ≤ L̄ < H(X)+1 bits per symbol, and the gap vanishes when you code long blocks. The Kraft inequality, Σ 2^(−ℓ_i) ≤ 1, characterizes exactly which sets of codeword lengths admit a uniquely decodable prefix code.
depths.deep: Optimal codeword lengths are ℓ_i ≈ −log2 p_i, recovering surprise as code length. Huffman coding achieves the optimal integer-length prefix code; arithmetic coding approaches the entropy bound to within o(1) bits per symbol by escaping the integer-length constraint. Kraft's inequality is what forbids 'free lunch': shortening one codeword forces lengthening others.

sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
atoms.art_prompt: frequent symbols wearing short codeword tags and rare symbols wearing long ones, with a meter pinned at the entropy floor

quiz.prompt: What lower bound does the source coding theorem place on the average length of any lossless code?
quiz.answer: The entropy H(X): no uniquely decodable code can have average length below H(X) bits per symbol.

quiz.prompt: Can codeword lengths {1, 2, 2, 3} form a valid binary prefix code? Use Kraft.
quiz.answer: Σ 2^(−ℓ) = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/8 = 9/8 > 1, so no — it violates the Kraft inequality.

atoms.title: Mutual information
atoms.summary: Mutual information is the number of bits one variable reveals about another — the reduction in uncertainty from observing it.

depths.eli5: If knowing Y makes you less unsure about X, that shared knowledge is the mutual information. If they're unrelated, it's zero.
depths.core: I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) measures how much observing Y reduces uncertainty about X. It is symmetric, nonnegative, and zero exactly when X and Y are independent. Equivalently it is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the joint distribution and the product of the marginals, quantifying how far they are from independence.
depths.deep: I(X;Y) ≥ 0 follows from the convexity of KL divergence (Gibbs' inequality). The data-processing inequality says no clever post-processing of Y can increase the information it carries about X: if X→Y→Z is a Markov chain then I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y). This is the formal reason you cannot manufacture information by computation alone.

atoms.note: Mutual information is the rate quantity behind channel capacity, feature selection, and the information bottleneck in deep learning.
sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Mutual information; Data processing inequality
atoms.art_prompt: two overlapping uncertainty circles whose intersection is shaded and labeled I(X;Y), with the union labeled H(X,Y)

quiz.prompt: When is the mutual information I(X;Y) exactly zero?
quiz.answer: Exactly when X and Y are statistically independent.

quiz.prompt: State the data-processing inequality for a Markov chain X→Y→Z and say what it forbids.
quiz.answer: I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y); post-processing Y into Z cannot create information about X that Y did not already carry.

atoms.title: Channel capacity and the noisy-channel coding theorem
atoms.summary: Every noisy channel has a maximum reliable rate, the capacity C, below which error can be driven to zero and above which it cannot.

depths.eli5: Even on a noisy line, there's a top speed at which you can talk and still be understood perfectly if you encode cleverly. Push past it and mistakes become unavoidable.
depths.core: The capacity of a channel is the maximum mutual information between its input and output over all input distributions: C = max_p(x) I(X;Y). Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem says any rate R < C is achievable with arbitrarily small error using long block codes, and any rate R > C has error bounded away from zero. Reliable communication and the noise floor are thus a single number.
depths.deep: The achievability proof is non-constructive: it uses random codebooks and 'typical set' decoding to show good codes exist, without naming one. Closing the gap to capacity with explicit, efficiently decodable codes took decades — turbo codes, LDPC, and polar codes (the first provably capacity-achieving family for symmetric channels) finally did it. Capacity separates source and channel coding: you can compress to entropy, then protect to capacity, independently.

atoms.note: For a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p, C = 1 − H(p) bits per use, where H(p) is the binary entropy function.
sources: Wikipedia (facts): Noisy-channel coding theorem; Channel capacity
atoms.art_prompt: a pipe with noise sprayed across it and a throughput gauge pinned at C, with a clean signal flowing below the line and garbled above it

quiz.prompt: What does Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem say about rates below capacity C?
quiz.answer: Any rate R < C is achievable with arbitrarily small probability of error using sufficiently long codes.

quiz.prompt: A binary symmetric channel flips each bit with probability p = 0.11. Roughly what is its capacity?
quiz.answer: C = 1 − H(0.11) ≈ 1 − 0.5 = 0.5 bits per channel use.

atoms.title: Error-correcting codes and Hamming distance
atoms.summary: By spreading codewords far apart in Hamming distance, a code can detect and correct a bounded number of bit errors.

depths.eli5: If valid messages are very different from each other, a few flipped bits still leave one obvious nearest valid message. So you snap a corrupted message back to it.
depths.core: A code maps messages to codewords separated by minimum Hamming distance d_min (the fewest bit positions in which two codewords differ). A code can detect up to d_min − 1 errors and correct up to t = ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋ errors, because any received word within t flips of a unique codeword decodes to it. Linear codes (Hamming, Reed–Solomon, LDPC) make encoding and decoding efficient via algebra.
depths.deep: Coding is a sphere-packing problem in Hamming space: nonoverlapping balls of radius t around each codeword. The Hamming bound limits how many codewords fit; the Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees a minimum density exists. Shannon's capacity is the asymptotic ceiling these combinatorial bounds approach. Reed–Solomon codes underlie CDs, QR codes, and deep-space links; LDPC and polar codes power modern wireless.

sources: MIT OCW 6.02 Introduction to EECS II
Wikipedia (facts): Hamming distance; Hamming bound; Reed–Solomon
atoms.art_prompt: codewords as points in a grid each surrounded by a protective sphere of radius t, with a corrupted point snapping to its nearest center

quiz.prompt: A code has minimum Hamming distance d_min = 7. How many bit errors can it correct?
Explain why large minimum distance lets a code correct errors.
quiz.answer: If valid codewords are far apart, a small number of flipped bits keeps the received word closest to exactly one codeword, so decoding to the nearest codeword recovers the original.

atoms.title: Kolmogorov complexity
atoms.summary: The complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program that prints it — the algorithmic, per-object version of information.

depths.eli5: How short can a recipe be that produces exactly this string? A million repeated 'ab' has a tiny recipe; a million truly random coin flips has no recipe shorter than itself.
depths.core: K(x) is the length of the shortest program (on a fixed universal Turing machine U) that outputs x and halts. Unlike Shannon entropy, which describes a distribution, K describes a single object. The invariance theorem guarantees that switching universal machines changes K by at most an additive constant, so K is well-defined up to that constant. A string is 'random' (incompressible) when K(x) ≈ |x|.
depths.deep: K is not computable: no algorithm outputs K(x) for all x, and Chaitin's theorem sharpens this — any consistent formal system can prove 'K(x) > c' for only finitely many x, no matter how large the true values get. This is Gödel incompleteness in information-theoretic dress. The expected Kolmogorov complexity of strings drawn from a computable distribution equals its Shannon entropy up to a constant, tying the two notions of information together.

atoms.note: Most strings are incompressible by a simple counting argument: there are 2^n strings of length n but fewer than 2^n programs shorter than n, so most strings have no short description.
sources: Li & Vitányi, An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity (facts)
atoms.art_prompt: two strings side by side — a regular repeating pattern with a tiny program tag, and random noise whose program tag is as long as the string itself

quiz.prompt: What guarantees that Kolmogorov complexity is well-defined despite depending on a choice of machine?
quiz.answer: The invariance theorem: any two universal machines give K values differing by at most an additive constant independent of x.

quiz.prompt: In one or two sentences, why is K(x) not computable?
quiz.answer: If you could compute K, you could search for and print the first string whose complexity exceeds the length of your own program — a contradiction (the Berry-paradox/Chaitin argument), so no such algorithm exists.

atoms.title: Sets, functions, and relations
atoms.summary: Sets are collections; functions map each input to one output; relations are any set of input–output pairs — the vocabulary of all formal definitions.

depths.eli5: A set is a bag of things. A function is a machine that gives exactly one answer per input. A relation is looser — it can link an input to many things.
depths.core: A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. A function f: A→B assigns to each element of the domain A exactly one element of the codomain B; a relation on A×B is any subset of ordered pairs, so every function is a relation but not vice versa. Cardinality measures size, and a function is a bijection (perfect pairing) iff it is both injective and surjective.
depths.deep: Countable vs. uncountable hinges on bijection: a set is countable if it can be put in bijection with a subset of the naturals. Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals (and the set of all languages over an alphabet) are uncountable, while the set of programs is only countable — the seed of why most functions are uncomputable.

sources: MIT OCW 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: an arrow diagram where each domain dot sends exactly one arrow (a function) beside a looser web of arrows (a general relation)

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a function from a general relation?
quiz.answer: A function assigns each domain element exactly one output; a general relation may pair an element with zero, one, or many.

quiz.prompt: Why are there 'more' functions/languages than programs?
quiz.answer: Programs are finite strings, so they are countable; the set of all languages over an alphabet is uncountable (Cantor diagonalization), so most languages have no program — most functions are uncomputable.

atoms.title: Finite automata (DFA and NFA)
atoms.summary: A finite automaton is a machine with finitely many states that reads input symbol by symbol and accepts or rejects.

depths.eli5: Imagine a board game with a few squares. Each letter you read tells you which square to hop to. If you end on a 'win' square, the word is accepted.
depths.core: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) has a finite set of states, a transition function moving to exactly one next state per input symbol, a start state, and accepting states. A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) may branch to several states (or none) and accepts if any branch reaches an accept state. DFAs and NFAs recognize exactly the same class — the regular languages.
depths.deep: The subset construction converts any NFA with n states into an equivalent DFA with up to 2^n states, proving the equivalence but exposing an exponential state blowup. Finite automata have no memory beyond their current state, which is exactly why they cannot count unboundedly — the limitation the pumping lemma formalizes.

atoms.note: Regular expressions, DFAs, and NFAs are three faces of the same expressive power: the regular languages.
sources: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (definitions/facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Deterministic finite automaton; Subset construction
atoms.art_prompt: a state diagram with labeled circles and arrows, one path traced deterministically and another fanning out into parallel nondeterministic branches

quiz.prompt: Do NFAs recognize more languages than DFAs?
quiz.answer: No — they recognize exactly the same class, the regular languages; the subset construction converts any NFA into an equivalent DFA.

quiz.prompt: An NFA has 4 states. What is the worst-case number of states in an equivalent DFA from the subset construction?
quiz.answer: 2^4 = 16 states.

atoms.title: Regular languages and the pumping lemma
atoms.summary: Regular languages are exactly those recognized by finite automata; the pumping lemma proves some languages are not regular.

depths.eli5: Finite-memory machines can recognize lots of patterns, but they can't truly count. So 'equal numbers of A's then B's' is beyond them — and there's a trick to prove it.
depths.core: A language is regular iff some DFA recognizes it. The pumping lemma states that for any regular language there is a length p such that every string of length ≥ p can be split xyz with y nonempty and within the first p symbols, where xy^i z stays in the language for all i ≥ 0. If no such p works, the language is not regular — the standard tool for proving languages like {0^n 1^n} lie outside the regular class.
depths.deep: The pumping lemma is really the pigeonhole principle on states: a long enough accepted string forces the automaton to revisit a state, creating a loop (the y part) you can traverse any number of times. The lemma is necessary but not sufficient for regularity, so a clean proof of non-regularity must show the pumping condition fails for every choice of decomposition.

sources: Wikipedia (facts): Pumping lemma for regular languages
atoms.art_prompt: an automaton path that loops through a repeated state, with the loop segment highlighted as the 'pumpable' middle of a string

quiz.prompt: Why can't a finite automaton recognize {0^n 1^n : n ≥ 0}?
quiz.answer: It would need to remember n, but finite states can hold only bounded memory; the pumping lemma formalizes this — pumping the loop breaks the equal-count requirement.

quiz.prompt: What principle underlies the pumping lemma?
quiz.answer: The pigeonhole principle: a sufficiently long accepted string must revisit a state, forming a loop that can be repeated.

atoms.title: Context-free languages and grammars
atoms.summary: Context-free grammars generate nested, recursive structure (like balanced parentheses) that finite automata cannot.

depths.eli5: Rules like 'a sentence can contain a smaller sentence inside it' let you build nested structures — matching brackets, math expressions, programming languages.
depths.core: A context-free grammar (CFG) has production rules rewriting a single nonterminal into a string of terminals and nonterminals. CFGs generate the context-free languages, recognized by pushdown automata — finite automata equipped with a stack. The stack supplies exactly the bounded-recursion memory needed for balanced nesting like {0^n 1^n} and the syntax of programming languages.
depths.deep: There is a pumping lemma for context-free languages too, with two pumpable segments instead of one, proving that languages like {0^n 1^n 2^n} are not context-free. Parsing a CFG can be done in polynomial time (CYK algorithm, O(n^3)); deterministic CFGs admit linear-time parsers, which is why real compilers restrict grammars to LL/LR subclasses.

atoms.note: Pushdown automata = finite automaton + one stack. Adding a second stack (or a tape) jumps all the way to Turing-machine power.
sources: Wikipedia (facts): Context-free grammar; Pushdown automaton; CYK algorithm
atoms.art_prompt: a parse tree of balanced parentheses growing recursively, with a stack beside it pushing and popping symbols

quiz.prompt: What machine model recognizes exactly the context-free languages?
quiz.answer: Pushdown automata — finite automata augmented with a single stack.

quiz.prompt: Is {0^n 1^n 2^n : n ≥ 0} context-free?
quiz.answer: No; it fails the context-free pumping lemma — a single stack cannot match three counts simultaneously.

atoms.title: The Chomsky hierarchy
atoms.summary: Languages stratify into four nested classes — regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable — each tied to a machine model.

depths.eli5: There's a ladder of grammar power. Each rung can describe more complicated patterns than the one below, and needs a more powerful machine to recognize it.
depths.core: Chomsky classified grammars into Type 3 (regular, finite automata), Type 2 (context-free, pushdown automata), Type 1 (context-sensitive, linear-bounded automata), and Type 0 (recursively enumerable, Turing machines). The language classes are strictly nested: each inclusion is proper, so adding the right kind of memory to a machine strictly increases what it can recognize.
depths.deep: The hierarchy is a memory ladder: no memory (finite states) → one stack (pushdown) → tape bounded by input length (linear-bounded) → unbounded tape (Turing machine). The jump from Type 1 to Type 0 is the jump from 'always halts' to 'may run forever' — context-sensitive languages are decidable, while recursively enumerable languages are only semi-decidable.

atoms.art_prompt: four nested boxes labeled regular, context-free, context-sensitive, recursively enumerable, each paired with its machine icon

quiz.prompt: List the four levels of the Chomsky hierarchy from least to most powerful and their machine models.
quiz.answer: Regular (finite automaton) ⊂ context-free (pushdown automaton) ⊂ context-sensitive (linear-bounded automaton) ⊂ recursively enumerable (Turing machine).

quiz.prompt: What single resource distinguishes the levels of the hierarchy?
quiz.answer: Memory: none, one stack, a tape bounded by input size, and finally an unbounded tape.

atoms.title: The Turing machine
atoms.summary: A Turing machine is a finite controller with an unbounded tape — the standard mathematical model of any computation.

depths.eli5: Picture an endless paper strip and a little head that reads a symbol, writes a symbol, and steps left or right based on simple rules. That tiny device can compute anything a computer can.
depths.core: A Turing machine has a finite set of states, a read/write head, and an infinite tape. At each step it reads the current symbol and, per its transition rule, writes a symbol, moves left or right, and changes state, halting when it reaches an accept/reject state. Despite its simplicity it can simulate any algorithm — its unbounded tape supplies the unlimited memory finite automata and pushdown automata lack.
depths.deep: A universal Turing machine takes the description of another machine plus an input and simulates it — the theoretical basis of the stored-program computer. Variations (multi-tape, nondeterministic, multi-track) are all equivalent in computing power to the basic single-tape model, differing only by polynomial-time overhead. The model fixes what 'computable' means precisely enough to prove things are impossible.

atoms.note: All reasonable models of computation — lambda calculus, register machines, cellular automata, your laptop — compute exactly the same functions as the Turing machine.
sources: Wikipedia (facts): Turing machine; Universal Turing machine
atoms.art_prompt: an infinite tape with a small read/write head poised over a cell, a state label above it, and a rule table beside it

quiz.prompt: What gives a Turing machine its power beyond a pushdown automaton?
quiz.answer: An unbounded, read/write tape — unlimited random-access-like memory rather than a single stack.

quiz.prompt: What is a universal Turing machine and why does it matter?
quiz.answer: A machine that takes a description of any other machine plus its input and simulates it; it is the abstract model of a general-purpose, stored-program computer.

atoms.title: The Church–Turing thesis
atoms.summary: Anything effectively computable by any mechanical procedure is computable by a Turing machine — the definition of 'computable'.

depths.eli5: Every honest step-by-step method you could ever follow can be done by a Turing machine. So 'a computer can do it' and 'there's a procedure for it' mean the same thing.
depths.core: The Church–Turing thesis asserts that the intuitive notion of an 'effective procedure' coincides exactly with what Turing machines (equivalently, the lambda calculus, recursive functions, etc.) can compute. It is not a theorem but a definition-fixing claim, supported by the striking fact that every independently proposed model of computation has turned out to define the same class of computable functions.
depths.deep: The thesis is empirical/conceptual, not provable, because it equates a formal class with an informal idea. The 'physical' or 'extended' Church–Turing thesis goes further, claiming nature itself computes nothing a Turing machine cannot (in polynomial-time form, this is challenged by quantum computing). Hypercomputation models exist on paper but require physically unrealizable resources like infinite-precision reals or completed infinite processes.

sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Church–Turing Thesis
atoms.art_prompt: several different computing models — lambda terms, a register machine, a Turing tape — converging arrows into one labeled box 'the computable functions'

quiz.prompt: Is the Church–Turing thesis a theorem? Why or why not?
quiz.answer: No — it equates the informal idea of an effective procedure with a formal class, so it cannot be proven, only supported by evidence.

quiz.prompt: What evidence makes the thesis compelling?
quiz.answer: Every independently proposed model of computation (lambda calculus, recursive functions, register machines, etc.) defines exactly the same set of computable functions.

atoms.title: Decidability and recognizability
atoms.summary: A problem is decidable if some machine always halts with the right yes/no answer; merely recognizable if it halts on the yes-instances.

depths.eli5: Decidable means there's a method that always finishes and tells you yes or no. Recognizable is weaker: it says yes when the answer is yes, but might run forever when the answer is no.
depths.core: A language is decidable (recursive) if a Turing machine halts on every input and correctly accepts or rejects. It is recognizable (recursively enumerable) if a machine halts and accepts on every yes-instance but may loop forever on no-instances. A language is decidable iff both it and its complement are recognizable — the key bridge between the two notions.
depths.deep: Recognizable-but-undecidable problems are the heart of computability theory: the halting problem is recognizable (run the machine; if it halts, accept) but not decidable. Its complement is not even recognizable. This asymmetry — you can confirm halting but never, in general, confirm non-halting — is the source of most undecidability proofs via reduction.

atoms.art_prompt: two flowcharts — a decider that always reaches HALT, and a recognizer with one branch that loops forever on 'no' inputs

quiz.prompt: State the relationship between decidability and recognizability.
quiz.answer: A language is decidable iff both it and its complement are recognizable (recursively enumerable).

quiz.prompt: Why is the halting problem recognizable but not decidable?
quiz.answer: You can confirm a yes by simulating until it halts, but you can never be sure a non-halting machine won't eventually stop, so no machine decides it in all cases.

atoms.title: The halting problem
atoms.summary: No algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether that program eventually halts — the foundational undecidability result.

depths.eli5: You can't build a perfect 'will-this-program-finish?' checker. If you could, you could feed it a program designed to do the opposite of whatever the checker predicts, creating a contradiction.
depths.core: The halting problem asks: given a program P and input x, does P(x) halt? Turing proved no algorithm decides this for all inputs. The proof is by diagonalization: assume a decider H exists, build a program D that halts iff H says it loops, then run D on its own description to derive a contradiction. Halting is therefore undecidable, though it remains recognizable.
depths.deep: Halting is the canonical undecidable problem from which countless others are proven undecidable by reduction: if solving problem A would let you solve halting, then A is undecidable too. Rice's theorem generalizes this: every nontrivial semantic property of a program's input/output behavior is undecidable. Undecidability is thus pervasive, not exotic.

atoms.note: Rice's theorem: any nontrivial property of the language a program computes is undecidable — 'does this program ever output 42?' has no general algorithm.
atoms.art_prompt: a self-referential loop where a halting-checker box feeds into a program that inverts its own prediction, with a contradiction spark at the join

quiz.prompt: Sketch why a universal halting decider H leads to a contradiction.
quiz.answer: Build D that takes a program P and loops if H(P,P) says 'halts', else halts. Running D on D forces D to halt iff it loops — a contradiction, so H cannot exist.

quiz.prompt: What does Rice's theorem add to the halting result?
quiz.answer: It shows undecidability is generic: every nontrivial property of the function a program computes is undecidable, not just halting.

atoms.title: Asymptotic notation (big-O)
atoms.equation: f(n)=O(g(n))\iff \exists c,n_0:\ f(n)\le c\,g(n)\ \forall n\ge n_0
atoms.summary: Big-O captures how a cost grows with input size, ignoring constants and small inputs — the language of efficiency.

depths.eli5: We care how an algorithm slows down as the problem gets big, not exactly how many seconds it takes. Doubling the input might double the work, square it, or barely change it.
depths.core: f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g up to a constant factor for large n. Companion notations Ω (lower bound) and Θ (tight bound) frame matching ceilings and floors. This abstraction lets us compare algorithms by growth rate — O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n) — independent of hardware and constant factors.
depths.deep: Asymptotics can mislead when constants or low-order terms dominate at realistic input sizes (e.g., galactic algorithms with great big-O but absurd constants). Amortized and average-case analysis refine the worst-case picture; the gap between worst-case and typical-case behavior is exactly why simplex and quicksort thrive despite bad worst cases.

atoms.note: Memorize the ladder: constant ≪ logarithmic ≪ linear ≪ n log n ≪ quadratic ≪ exponential. Crossing from polynomial to exponential is the practical wall.
atoms.art_prompt: growth curves on one axis — flat log, straight line, gentle n log n, rising parabola, exploding exponential — diverging as n increases

quiz.prompt: Is 3n^2 + 100n + 7 equal to O(n^2)? Justify briefly.
quiz.answer: Yes; for large n the n^2 term dominates and the whole expression is bounded by c·n^2 (e.g., c = 4) for n beyond some n_0.

quiz.prompt: What do Ω and Θ denote relative to O?
quiz.answer: Ω is an asymptotic lower bound and Θ is a tight bound (both upper and lower), whereas O is an upper bound.

atoms.title: Divide and conquer
atoms.summary: Split a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine — the recipe behind mergesort and fast multiplication.

depths.eli5: Cut a big job into halves, solve each half the same way, then stitch the answers together. Sorting a deck by splitting, sorting each pile, and merging is the classic example.
depths.core: A divide-and-conquer algorithm breaks an input of size n into a subproblems of size n/b, recurses, and spends f(n) work to combine results, giving the recurrence T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n). The Master Theorem solves this recurrence by comparing f(n) to n^(log_b a): the larger term dominates the running time. Mergesort (a=2,b=2,f=n) gives Θ(n log n).
depths.deep: Divide and conquer wins when subproblems are independent and combining is cheap relative to the split. Karatsuba multiplication beats the schoolbook O(n^2) by reducing four subproducts to three (T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n) → O(n^1.585)); the FFT extends the idea to O(n log n) polynomial multiplication. When subproblems overlap instead, divide and conquer wastes work and dynamic programming is the right tool.

sources: Wikipedia (facts): Master theorem; Divide and conquer algorithm
atoms.art_prompt: a recursion tree halving an array at each level, with merge arrows recombining sorted halves from the leaves upward

quiz.prompt: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n using the Master Theorem.
quiz.answer: Here a=2, b=2 so n^(log_b a) = n; f(n)=n matches, giving T(n) = Θ(n log n).

quiz.prompt: When does divide and conquer become wasteful, and what replaces it?
quiz.answer: When subproblems overlap and get recomputed; dynamic programming, which stores subproblem answers, replaces it.

atoms.title: Dynamic programming
atoms.summary: Solve overlapping subproblems once and reuse the answers, turning exponential brute force into polynomial time.

depths.eli5: If the same little subproblem keeps coming up, solve it once and write the answer down. Don't recompute it a thousand times.
depths.core: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure (its optimum is built from subproblem optima) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur). You define a recurrence over states, then fill a table bottom-up (or memoize top-down) so each state is computed once. Fibonacci, shortest paths, edit distance, and knapsack are canonical examples.
depths.deep: The art is choosing the right state space so the recurrence is correct and small. Complexity is roughly (number of states) × (work per transition). Bellman's principle of optimality justifies the recurrence; for shortest paths it yields Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall. Many DPs can be sped up further with monotonicity tricks (convex-hull, Knuth, divide-and-conquer optimization).

atoms.note: Two ingredients are mandatory: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Without overlap, plain divide and conquer suffices; without optimal substructure, DP is invalid.
