quiz.prompt: What two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to apply?
quiz.answer: Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.

quiz.prompt: Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential. Why does memoization make it linear?
quiz.answer: Each Fib(k) is computed once and cached; there are n distinct subproblems with O(1) work each, giving O(n).

atoms.title: Graphs and graph search
atoms.summary: Graphs model relationships as vertices and edges; BFS and DFS explore them, underpinning shortest paths, connectivity, and ordering.

depths.eli5: A graph is dots connected by lines — cities and roads, people and friendships. To explore it you either spread out level by level (BFS) or dive deep down one path then backtrack (DFS).
depths.core: A graph G = (V, E) has vertices V and edges E, directed or undirected, weighted or not. Breadth-first search explores in layers and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first search recurses along edges and reveals connectivity, cycles, and topological order. Dijkstra's algorithm extends BFS to nonnegative weights using a priority queue, running in O((V+E) log V).
depths.deep: Graph problems span the difficulty spectrum: shortest path and minimum spanning tree are polynomial, while Hamiltonian cycle and graph coloring are NP-complete. The same input can be easy or hard depending on the question — Eulerian (every edge once) is linear-time, Hamiltonian (every vertex once) is NP-complete, despite their superficial similarity.

atoms.art_prompt: a graph of dots and edges with a BFS wavefront spreading in concentric rings beside a DFS path plunging deep and backtracking

quiz.prompt: Which traversal finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph, and which reveals topological order?
quiz.answer: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS yields topological order (on a DAG).

quiz.prompt: Why can't plain BFS find shortest paths when edges have different positive weights?
quiz.answer: BFS counts edges, not weights, so a path with more low-weight edges can be cheaper than a few heavy ones; Dijkstra's priority queue handles weights.

atoms.title: Hashing and core data structures
atoms.summary: Data structures trade memory for speed; hash tables give expected O(1) lookup by scattering keys across buckets.

depths.eli5: A hash table is like a coat-check: a quick formula turns your ticket into a hook number, so you find your coat instantly instead of searching every hook.
depths.core: Choosing a data structure means choosing which operations are fast: arrays give O(1) indexing, balanced trees give O(log n) ordered queries, heaps give O(log n) priority access, and hash tables give expected O(1) insert/lookup by mapping keys to buckets via a hash function. Collisions (two keys, one bucket) are resolved by chaining or open addressing.
depths.deep: Hash-table guarantees are probabilistic and rest on the hash spreading keys uniformly; with universal hashing, expected collisions stay O(1) regardless of the input, defeating adversaries who would otherwise force O(n) worst cases. The space–time tradeoff is fundamental: Bloom filters shrink memory at the cost of false positives, and cuckoo/perfect hashing buy worst-case O(1) lookups at extra construction cost.

atoms.note: Worst-case for a naive hash table is O(n) per operation; universal/randomized hashing restores expected O(1) even against adversarial inputs.
sources: Wikipedia (facts): Hash table; Universal hashing; Bloom filter
atoms.art_prompt: keys flying through a hash function into numbered buckets, with a collision chain hanging off one bucket

quiz.prompt: What is the expected and worst-case lookup time of a hash table?
quiz.answer: Expected O(1); worst case O(n) (all keys colliding), mitigated by universal hashing.

quiz.prompt: Why prefer a balanced binary search tree over a hash table for some tasks?
quiz.answer: Trees keep keys ordered, enabling range queries, successor/predecessor, and sorted traversal in O(log n) — operations hash tables cannot do efficiently.

atoms.title: The class P (efficient computation)
atoms.summary: P is the class of problems a deterministic machine solves in polynomial time — the standard formal notion of 'tractable'.

depths.eli5: P is the set of problems a computer can solve reasonably fast — the work grows like the size raised to some fixed power, not explosively.
depths.core: A decision problem is in P if some deterministic Turing machine decides it in time O(n^k) for a constant k. Polynomial time is the robust dividing line between tractable and intractable: it is closed under composition and stable across all reasonable machine models (the Cobham–Edmonds thesis), so 'polynomial' means the same thing whether you count tape steps or laptop operations.
depths.deep: Polynomial time is a deliberate idealization — an O(n^100) algorithm is 'efficient' in theory but useless in practice, while some exponential algorithms run fine on real inputs. Yet the polynomial/exponential boundary remains the right theoretical cut because it is model-independent and composition-stable, which finer constant-sensitive definitions are not. Sorting, shortest paths, and primality testing all live comfortably in P.

atoms.art_prompt: a clock whose hand sweeps along a polynomial curve as input grows, staying within a tractable shaded band

quiz.prompt: Define the complexity class P.
quiz.answer: Decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the input size.

quiz.prompt: Why is 'polynomial time' the chosen line for tractability despite O(n^100) being impractical?
quiz.answer: It is robust — model-independent and closed under composition — whereas constant-sensitive definitions are not; the polynomial/exponential gap is the stable theoretical boundary.

atoms.title: The class NP and verification
atoms.summary: NP is the class of problems whose 'yes' answers have short certificates checkable in polynomial time.

depths.eli5: NP problems are ones where finding the answer might be hard, but checking a proposed answer is fast — like a jigsaw: hard to solve, instant to verify once assembled.
depths.core: A problem is in NP if every yes-instance has a certificate (witness) of polynomial size that a deterministic verifier can check in polynomial time. Equivalently, NP is what a nondeterministic Turing machine decides in polynomial time. P ⊆ NP, since solving outright also lets you verify; whether the inclusion is strict is the P vs NP question.
depths.deep: NP is fundamentally about asymmetry between finding and checking. The complement class co-NP concerns short certificates for no-instances; whether NP = co-NP is open and tied to whether short proofs of unsatisfiability always exist. Most natural search problems where solutions are recognizable but seemingly require search — SAT, clique, scheduling — live in NP.

atoms.note: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP. Each inclusion is believed strict; only P ⊊ EXP is currently proven (by the time hierarchy theorem).
atoms.art_prompt: a maze that is hard to solve from the entrance but, given a highlighted solution path, instantly checkable as valid

quiz.prompt: Give the verifier-based definition of NP.
quiz.answer: Problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-size certificates checkable by a deterministic verifier in polynomial time.

quiz.prompt: Why is P ⊆ NP immediate?
quiz.answer: If you can solve a problem in polynomial time, you can verify any claimed answer in polynomial time (just re-solve), so every P problem is in NP.

atoms.title: Polynomial-time reductions
atoms.summary: A reduction transforms one problem into another in polynomial time, transferring tractability and hardness between them.

depths.eli5: If you can quickly rewrite problem A as problem B, then a solver for B solves A too. So A is 'no harder than' B.
depths.core: A polynomial-time many-one reduction from A to B is a poly-time map f turning instances of A into instances of B with the same yes/no answer, written A ≤_p B. It means A is no harder than B (up to polynomial factors): if B ∈ P then A ∈ P, and contrapositively, if A is hard then B is hard. Reductions are the algebra of computational difficulty.
depths.deep: Reductions are transitive (A ≤_p B and B ≤_p C imply A ≤_p C), which is what lets a single hard problem certify the hardness of thousands of others. The direction matters: to prove B is hard you reduce a known-hard A to B (A ≤_p B), not the reverse — a common pitfall. Turing reductions (oracle access) are more permissive than many-one and define different completeness notions.

atoms.art_prompt: an arrow labeled f converting an instance of problem A into an instance of problem B, with a 'same answer' stamp across the transformation

quiz.prompt: To prove problem B is hard, which direction of reduction do you use, and why?
quiz.answer: Reduce a known-hard problem A to B (A ≤_p B): if B were easy, A would be too, contradicting A's hardness — so B must be hard.

quiz.prompt: If A ≤_p B and B ∈ P, what follows about A?
quiz.answer: A ∈ P — tractability transfers from B back to A through the reduction.

atoms.title: NP-completeness and Cook–Levin
atoms.summary: The NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; Boolean satisfiability was the first, and a fast algorithm for any one would crack them all.

depths.eli5: Some NP problems are universal: solving one quickly would solve every NP problem quickly. SAT — deciding if a logical formula can be made true — is the original such problem.
depths.core: A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. The Cook–Levin theorem proved SAT is NP-complete by encoding a nondeterministic machine's computation as a Boolean formula. Karp then showed dozens of natural problems (3-SAT, clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, knapsack) are NP-complete by reduction. A polynomial algorithm for any one would put all of NP in P.
depths.deep: NP-completeness explains why thousands of practically important problems resist efficient solution: they are all the 'same' problem in disguise, linked by a web of reductions back to SAT. This is why P vs NP is the central open question — proving P ≠ NP would confirm these problems are genuinely intractable; proving P = NP would collapse the distinction and break modern cryptography. In practice, NP-hardness signals to switch to approximation, heuristics, or special cases.

atoms.note: P vs NP carries a $1M Clay Millennium Prize. Almost all experts conjecture P ≠ NP, but no proof exists.
atoms.art_prompt: SAT as a central hub with reduction arrows fanning out to clique, knapsack, coloring, and Hamiltonian cycle, all sharing one hardness core

quiz.prompt: What two conditions make a problem NP-complete?
quiz.answer: It is in NP, and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time (NP-hardness).

quiz.prompt: Why would a polynomial algorithm for 3-SAT imply P = NP?
quiz.answer: Every NP problem reduces to 3-SAT in polynomial time, so solving 3-SAT fast would solve all of NP fast, collapsing NP into P.

atoms.title: Space complexity and PSPACE
atoms.summary: Measuring memory instead of time gives the classes L, PSPACE, and the theorem that nondeterministic and deterministic space coincide up to squaring.

depths.eli5: Besides 'how long does it take?', we can ask 'how much scratch paper does it need?'. Some problems are easy on memory but slow, or vice versa.
depths.core: Space complexity counts the work-tape cells a machine uses. PSPACE is the class solvable in polynomial space (with unbounded time); it contains NP and equals the power of polynomial-space games and quantified Boolean formulas (TQBF is PSPACE-complete). Savitch's theorem shows nondeterministic space is at most squared deterministic space: NSPACE(s) ⊆ DSPACE(s^2), so PSPACE = NPSPACE.
depths.deep: Space is reusable in a way time is not, which is why nondeterminism is far weaker for space (Savitch) than it is believed to be for time (P vs NP). The chain L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP has every inclusion conjectured proper, yet only L ⊊ PSPACE and P ⊊ EXP are proven, via the space and time hierarchy theorems. The immense gaps we cannot yet separate are the frontier of complexity theory.

atoms.art_prompt: a nested band diagram L ⊂ P ⊂ NP ⊂ PSPACE ⊂ EXP, with the few proven strict separations marked and the rest dashed as open

quiz.prompt: What does Savitch's theorem say about nondeterministic vs deterministic space?
quiz.answer: NSPACE(s) ⊆ DSPACE(s^2): nondeterminism saves at most a squaring in space, so PSPACE = NPSPACE.

quiz.prompt: Why is nondeterminism much less powerful for space than it seems to be for time?
quiz.answer: Space can be reused/overwritten, so a deterministic machine can systematically search all nondeterministic paths with only quadratic extra space — no analogous trick is known for time.

atoms.title: Propositional logic
atoms.summary: Propositional logic combines true/false statements with connectives; truth tables decide validity by enumerating cases.

depths.eli5: Glue together yes/no facts with AND, OR, NOT, and 'if...then'. A truth table checks every combination of yes/no to see when the whole statement holds.
depths.core: Propositional logic builds formulas from atomic propositions and connectives (¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔). A formula is satisfiable if some assignment makes it true, valid (a tautology) if every assignment does, and a contradiction if none does. Truth tables decide all of these by brute force over 2^n rows; satisfiability of propositional formulas is the SAT problem at the root of NP-completeness.
depths.deep: Propositional logic is sound and complete: a formula is provable in a proper proof system iff it is a tautology (semantic truth and syntactic provability coincide). It is also decidable — truth tables always terminate — which is exactly what predicate logic loses. Normal forms (CNF, DNF) standardize formulas; converting to CNF is the gateway to SAT solvers and resolution.

sources: MIT OCW 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: a truth table grid filling in T/F columns under AND, OR, NOT, and implication for a small formula

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a satisfiable formula and a valid (tautology) formula?
quiz.answer: Satisfiable: true under at least one assignment; valid: true under every assignment.

quiz.prompt: Is (P → Q) ∨ (Q → P) a tautology?
quiz.answer: Yes — for any truth values, at least one of the two implications holds, so the disjunction is always true.

atoms.title: Predicate (first-order) logic
atoms.summary: First-order logic adds quantifiers and predicates over objects, gaining the expressive power to formalize mathematics — at the cost of decidability.

depths.eli5: Now you can say 'for all x' and 'there exists an x', and talk about properties of and relations among objects. That's enough to write down essentially all of math.
depths.core: First-order (predicate) logic extends propositional logic with variables ranging over a domain, predicates and functions, and the quantifiers ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists). It is expressive enough to axiomatize arithmetic, set theory, and most of mathematics. Gödel's completeness theorem shows its proof system is sound and complete: a sentence is provable iff it is true in every model.
depths.deep: Validity in first-order logic is undecidable (Church and Turing) but recursively enumerable — you can enumerate proofs but cannot always decide non-validity. This is the precise boundary: propositional logic is decidable, first-order logic is only semi-decidable. The completeness theorem (provable = universally true) must not be confused with the incompleteness theorems, which concern specific theories like arithmetic being unable to prove all their own truths.

atoms.note: Don't conflate Gödel's completeness theorem (about first-order logic's proof system) with his incompleteness theorems (about sufficiently strong arithmetic theories) — they point in opposite directions.
sources: MIT OCW 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Classical Logic
Wikipedia (facts): First-order logic; Gödel's completeness theorem
atoms.art_prompt: a domain of objects with ∀ and ∃ quantifier lassos selecting all-of versus some-of them, predicates coloring relationships between objects

quiz.prompt: What does Gödel's completeness theorem state about first-order logic?
quiz.answer: A sentence is provable in the proof system iff it is true in every model — provability and semantic validity coincide.

quiz.prompt: Contrast the decidability of propositional and first-order logic.
quiz.answer: Propositional validity is decidable (truth tables terminate); first-order validity is undecidable but recursively enumerable — proofs can be enumerated, but non-validity can't always be decided.

atoms.title: Proof systems and soundness/completeness
atoms.summary: A proof system is a set of axioms and inference rules; soundness means it proves only truths, completeness that it proves all of them.

depths.eli5: A proof system is a rulebook for deriving new true statements from old ones. A good rulebook never lies (sound) and can reach every truth in its world (complete).
depths.core: A formal proof system specifies axioms and inference rules (like modus ponens) that mechanically generate theorems. Soundness means every provable statement is true (no false theorems); completeness means every true statement is provable. Natural deduction, sequent calculus, and resolution are equivalent systems for first-order logic, all sound and complete for it.
depths.deep: Proof complexity asks not whether a proof exists but how long it must be: resolution requires exponential-length proofs for some unsatisfiable formulas (the pigeonhole principle), and whether short propositional proofs always exist (NP =? co-NP) is open. The Curry–Howard correspondence reveals proofs as programs and propositions as types, unifying logic and computation — constructing a proof is literally writing a program.

sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Proof Theory
atoms.art_prompt: an inference tree growing from axiom leaves upward to a theorem root, each step stamped by a named rule like modus ponens

quiz.prompt: Define soundness and completeness of a proof system.
quiz.answer: Soundness: every provable statement is true. Completeness: every true statement is provable.

quiz.prompt: What does the Curry–Howard correspondence identify?
quiz.answer: Proofs with programs and propositions with types — constructing a proof of a proposition is the same act as writing a program of that type.

atoms.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
atoms.summary: Any consistent, sufficiently strong formal system cannot prove all true statements about arithmetic, nor prove its own consistency.

depths.eli5: Any rulebook powerful enough to do arithmetic has true statements it can never prove. And it can't prove that it itself won't ever contradict itself.
depths.core: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem: any consistent, effectively axiomatized theory strong enough to encode arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The construction encodes 'this statement is unprovable' as an arithmetic sentence via Gödel numbering — a self-reference that is true precisely because it is unprovable. The second theorem: such a system cannot prove its own consistency (unless it is inconsistent).
depths.deep: The incompleteness theorems are deeply tied to undecidability: the unprovability of certain truths mirrors the halting problem's undecidability, and Chaitin recast incompleteness in terms of Kolmogorov complexity (no system can prove a string's complexity exceeds the system's own size). The lesson is not that math is broken but that truth outruns proof in any fixed formal system — there is no finite axiom set capturing all arithmetic truth.

atoms.note: First theorem: truth > provability. Second theorem: a consistent system can't certify its own consistency. Both require the system to be strong enough to do arithmetic.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
atoms.art_prompt: a self-referential sentence written in arithmetic that asserts its own unprovability, encircled by a formal system that cannot reach it

quiz.prompt: State Gödel's second incompleteness theorem.
quiz.answer: A consistent, sufficiently strong formal system cannot prove its own consistency.

quiz.prompt: How does the halting problem connect to incompleteness?
quiz.answer: Both stem from self-reference/diagonalization: undecidability of halting implies no consistent system can decide every arithmetic truth, since deciding them would solve halting.

atoms.title: One-way functions
atoms.summary: A one-way function is easy to compute but computationally hard to invert — the conjectured bedrock of modern cryptography.

depths.eli5: Some operations are like scrambling an egg: easy to do, practically impossible to undo. Cryptography needs functions like that.
depths.core: A one-way function f is computable in polynomial time, but no efficient algorithm can find a preimage of f(x) for random x (except with negligible probability). Their existence is unproven and would imply P ≠ NP, yet they are necessary and sufficient for most of cryptography — secure encryption, digital signatures, and pseudorandom generators all rest on them. Candidate examples are factoring-based and discrete-log-based functions.
depths.deep: Cryptography lives in average-case hardness, not worst-case: NP-hardness guarantees some hard instances, but cryptography needs functions hard on typical inputs. One-way functions formalize exactly that. They also bridge to pseudorandomness — a function computationally indistinguishable from random is the engine behind stream ciphers — and to Shannon's distinction between unconditional (information-theoretic) and computational security: one-time pads are unbreakable in principle, while practical crypto trades that for keys you can actually distribute.

atoms.note: The existence of one-way functions is the single most important open assumption in cryptography; it implies P ≠ NP but is believed to be strictly stronger.
sources: Katz & Lindell, Introduction to Modern Cryptography (facts)
atoms.art_prompt: a function arrow that is wide and easy going forward, but a narrow, fog-blocked tunnel going backward from output to input

quiz.prompt: What two properties define a one-way function?
quiz.answer: Easy (polynomial-time) to compute, but hard (no efficient algorithm) to invert on random inputs.

quiz.prompt: Why does cryptography need average-case rather than worst-case hardness?
quiz.answer: An attacker faces typical keys/messages, so a function must be hard on random inputs; worst-case (NP) hardness only guarantees some hard instances exist.

atoms.title: Public-key cryptography
atoms.summary: Public-key systems use a publishable encryption key and a secret decryption key, enabling secure communication without sharing secrets first.

depths.eli5: Everyone can have your open padlock to lock a box, but only you hold the key to open it. So strangers can send you secrets without ever meeting to agree on a password.
depths.core: Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography gives each party a public key (shared openly) and a private key (kept secret). Anyone can encrypt with the public key, but only the private-key holder can decrypt; reversing the roles yields digital signatures. RSA rests on the hardness of factoring large integers; Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve systems rest on the discrete-logarithm problem — both trapdoor one-way functions.
depths.deep: The breakthrough (Diffie–Hellman 1976, then RSA) solved the key-distribution problem that crippled symmetric crypto: parties establish a shared secret over a public channel. Security is computational and conditional — Shor's algorithm factors and computes discrete logs in polynomial time on a quantum computer, threatening RSA and ECC and driving the move to post-quantum cryptography based on lattice problems believed hard even for quantum machines.

sources: Wikipedia (facts): Public-key cryptography; RSA; Shor's algorithm
atoms.art_prompt: an open padlock distributed to many senders who snap shut their boxes, with a single private key on the recipient's side opening them

quiz.prompt: What hard problems underlie RSA and Diffie–Hellman respectively?
quiz.answer: RSA: integer factorization; Diffie–Hellman (and ECC): the discrete-logarithm problem.

quiz.prompt: Why does Shor's algorithm threaten public-key cryptography?
quiz.answer: It factors integers and solves discrete logs in polynomial time on a quantum computer, breaking the hardness assumptions RSA and ECC depend on — hence post-quantum cryptography.

atoms.title: Pseudorandomness
atoms.summary: A pseudorandom generator stretches a short seed into a long string no efficient test can distinguish from true randomness.

depths.eli5: From a tiny truly-random seed, a clever recipe makes a long stream that looks random to anyone without unlimited computing power. It isn't random, but no fast test can tell.
depths.core: A pseudorandom generator (PRG) maps a short random seed to a longer output that is computationally indistinguishable from uniform — no polynomial-time test can tell the difference with non-negligible advantage. PRGs exist if one-way functions do (Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby). They underpin stream ciphers, simulations, and derandomization, replacing scarce true randomness with cheap pseudorandom bits.
depths.deep: Pseudorandomness is randomness relative to an observer's computational power: a PRG output has low Kolmogorov complexity (it is generated by a short program) yet is operationally random to bounded adversaries — exposing that 'random' is not absolute but resource-relative. Derandomization conjectures (BPP = P, under strong circuit lower bounds) say true randomness may not help computation at all, only convenience.

sources: Wikipedia (facts): Pseudorandom generator; Hardness vs. randomness
atoms.art_prompt: a short seed feeding a gear-box that spins out a long bit-stream, with a bounded observer's test failing to distinguish it from true coin flips

quiz.prompt: What does it mean for a generator's output to be pseudorandom?
quiz.answer: No efficient (polynomial-time) test can distinguish it from a truly uniform random string with non-negligible advantage.

quiz.prompt: How does pseudorandomness show that 'random' is resource-relative?
quiz.answer: A PRG output is deterministic and low-complexity (a short program makes it), yet appears perfectly random to any computationally bounded observer — randomness depends on who is judging.

atoms.title: PAC learning
atoms.summary: PAC learning formalizes learning from examples: with high probability, output a hypothesis that is approximately correct on unseen data.

depths.eli5: Learning is: see a bunch of labeled examples, then guess a rule that's mostly right on new examples you've never seen — and be confident you got it mostly right.
depths.core: In Valiant's Probably Approximately Correct framework, a concept class is PAC-learnable if there is an algorithm that, for any target concept and any unknown distribution, draws a polynomial number of samples and outputs (with probability ≥ 1 − δ) a hypothesis with error ≤ ε. The two parameters separate accuracy (ε, 'approximately') from confidence (δ, 'probably'). Learnability is about generalizing from finite data, not memorizing it.
depths.deep: PAC makes the distribution-free demand: the learner must succeed for every input distribution, which is what makes the guarantees meaningful. The key insight is that generalization is possible only if the hypothesis class is restricted — an unrestricted learner can always fit the training data yet fail on new points. How much restriction is needed is captured exactly by the VC dimension.

atoms.art_prompt: a cloud of labeled training points with a candidate boundary drawn through them, and faded test points checking it generalizes

quiz.prompt: What do the parameters ε and δ control in PAC learning?
quiz.answer: ε bounds the hypothesis error ('approximately correct'); δ bounds the failure probability ('probably').

quiz.prompt: Why must the hypothesis class be restricted for learning to generalize?
quiz.answer: An unrestricted class can always fit the training data exactly while behaving arbitrarily on unseen points, giving no generalization guarantee; restriction limits this overfitting.

atoms.title: VC dimension
atoms.summary: The VC dimension measures a model's capacity by the largest set of points it can label in every possible way — it sets the sample size needed to learn.

depths.eli5: A model's 'power' is the biggest set of points it can fit no matter how you label them. More power means you need more examples before you can trust it on new data.
depths.core: A hypothesis class shatters a set of points if, for every possible labeling, some hypothesis in the class realizes it. The VC dimension is the size of the largest shatterable set. A class is PAC-learnable iff its VC dimension is finite, and the sample complexity scales as Θ((d/ε) + (1/ε)log(1/δ)) for VC dimension d — capacity directly determines how many examples you need.
depths.deep: VC dimension explains the bias–variance tradeoff quantitatively: high capacity can fit anything (low bias) but demands more data to generalize (high variance), formalizing Occam's razor — simpler classes generalize from fewer examples. For example, axis-aligned half-lines on the real line have VC dimension 1, intervals 2, and linear separators in d dimensions have VC dimension d+1. A class that shatters arbitrarily large sets (infinite VC dimension) is not PAC-learnable at all.

atoms.note: Finite VC dimension is exactly the condition for distribution-free PAC learnability — the fundamental theorem of statistical learning.
atoms.art_prompt: four points on a plane with a linear separator achieving each of their labelings except one impossible XOR-like pattern, marking the capacity limit

quiz.prompt: What does it mean for a hypothesis class to shatter a set of points?
quiz.answer: For every possible labeling of those points, some hypothesis in the class realizes that exact labeling.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how does PAC sample complexity scale with VC dimension d and accuracy ε?
quiz.answer: About Θ((d/ε) + (1/ε)log(1/δ)) samples — linear in the VC dimension.

atoms.title: Entropy bridges information and statistical mechanics
atoms.summary: Shannon's information entropy and Boltzmann/Gibbs thermodynamic entropy are the same functional, linking bits to physical energy.

depths.eli5: The 'disorder' physicists measure in a gas and the 'uncertainty' information theorists measure in a message are the very same formula, just in different units.
depths.core: Gibbs entropy S = −k_B Σ p_i ln p_i and Shannon entropy H = −Σ p_i log2 p_i are identical up to the unit constant k_B and the logarithm base. Jaynes recast statistical mechanics as inference: the equilibrium distribution is the maximum-entropy distribution consistent with known constraints (like average energy), recovering the Boltzmann distribution as the least-biased guess. Landauer's principle then assigns a physical energy cost k_B T ln 2 to erasing one bit.
depths.deep: The identification turns thermodynamics into a special case of information theory: temperature is a Lagrange multiplier on the energy constraint, and the partition function is a normalizer. Landauer's bound (and Bennett's resolution of Maxwell's demon) shows information is physical — logically irreversible erasure must dissipate heat — closing the loop between computation, entropy, and the second law. The same maximum-entropy principle reappears in machine learning as the logistic/softmax model and in statistics as exponential families.

atoms.note: Landauer's principle: erasing one bit costs at least k_B T ln 2 ≈ 0.018 eV of dissipated energy at room temperature — the thermodynamic price of forgetting.
sources: Jaynes, 'Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics' (1957, facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Entropy (information theory); Landauer's principle; Maximum entropy thermodynamics
atoms.art_prompt: a box of gas microstates beside a stream of message symbols, both feeding the identical −Σ p log p formula, with a heat puff labeled kT ln2 as a bit is erased

quiz.prompt: State Landauer's principle and its significance.
quiz.answer: Erasing one bit dissipates at least k_B T ln 2 of energy as heat — information processing has an irreducible thermodynamic cost; information is physical.

quiz.prompt: How does Jaynes' maximum-entropy view recover the Boltzmann distribution?
quiz.answer: It picks the least-biased distribution consistent with the known average energy by maximizing entropy under that constraint, which yields the exponential Boltzmann form.

atoms.title: Modern machine learning — a glimpse
atoms.summary: Deep networks fit huge parametric functions by gradient descent, and their surprising generalization stretches classical learning theory.

depths.eli5: A neural network is a giant adjustable function. You nudge its millions of knobs a little at a time to reduce its mistakes, and somehow it learns to handle examples it never saw.
depths.core: A neural network composes layers of linear maps and nonlinearities into a function with millions or billions of parameters. Training minimizes a loss by gradient descent, with gradients computed efficiently via backpropagation — itself a dynamic-programming reuse of the chain rule across layers. The classical VC story predicts such over-parameterized models should overfit, yet they generalize well, which modern theory (implicit regularization, the double-descent curve) is still working to explain.
depths.deep: Backpropagation is exactly dynamic programming on the computation graph: each partial derivative is computed once and reused, giving cost linear in the network size rather than exponential. The frontier puzzle is generalization in the over-parameterized regime where parameters far exceed data — classical uniform-convergence bounds (VC, Rademacher) are vacuous there, so capacity alone no longer explains learning. The information-bottleneck view and links back to statistical mechanics (energy landscapes, phase transitions in learning) are active attempts to rebuild the theory.

atoms.note: Backprop = reverse-mode automatic differentiation = dynamic programming over the chain rule. The same idea, three names across three fields.
sources: MIT OCW 6.036 / 6.390 Introduction to Machine Learning
arXiv: Belkin et al., 'Reconciling modern ML and the bias–variance trade-off' (double descent, facts)
atoms.art_prompt: a layered network with arrows flowing forward to a loss and gradient arrows flowing backward reusing cached values, beside a double-descent test-error curve dipping twice

quiz.prompt: In what sense is backpropagation a dynamic-programming algorithm?
quiz.answer: It computes each intermediate derivative once and reuses it across the computation graph (reverse-mode autodiff), making total gradient cost linear in network size instead of exponential.

quiz.prompt: Why do over-parameterized deep networks challenge classical VC-based learning theory?
quiz.answer: They have enormous capacity (huge VC dimension) yet generalize well, while classical uniform-convergence bounds predict overfitting — so capacity alone fails to explain their success.

atoms.title: Randomized algorithms
atoms.summary: Algorithms that flip coins can be simpler and faster than deterministic ones, trading certainty for high-probability correctness or speed.

depths.eli5: Sometimes letting an algorithm make random choices makes it faster or simpler, while still being almost always right — like picking a random pivot to sort quickly.
depths.core: Randomized algorithms use random bits during execution. Las Vegas algorithms (like randomized quicksort) always return the correct answer with random running time; Monte Carlo algorithms (like Miller–Rabin primality testing) run in fixed time but may err with small, controllable probability. Randomization often dodges worst-case adversarial inputs and simplifies design, defining the complexity class BPP (bounded-error polynomial time).
depths.deep: The power of randomness is subtle: under widely believed circuit lower bounds, BPP = P, meaning randomness buys convenience and speed but not fundamentally more solvable problems (derandomization via pseudorandom generators). Yet randomization is provably essential in other models — distributed consensus, communication complexity, and cryptography rely on it irreducibly. The gap between 'random helps' and 'random is necessary' tracks the model.

sources: MIT OCW 6.046 Design and Analysis of Algorithms
atoms.art_prompt: an algorithm branching on coin flips, with a Las Vegas path always reaching the right answer and a Monte Carlo path mostly right with a small error fork

quiz.prompt: Distinguish Las Vegas from Monte Carlo randomized algorithms.
quiz.answer: Las Vegas: always correct, random running time. Monte Carlo: fixed running time, small probability of error.

quiz.prompt: What does the conjecture BPP = P suggest about the power of randomness?
quiz.answer: That randomness gives convenience and speed but not extra computational power — efficient deterministic algorithms could (under strong lower bounds) replace randomized ones via derandomization.

atoms.title: Kullback–Leibler divergence
atoms.summary: KL divergence measures the extra bits wasted when you encode data from p using a code optimized for q.

depths.eli5: If you build your compression assuming the world is q, but it's really p, you waste some bits. KL divergence counts exactly how many you waste.
depths.core: The Kullback–Leibler divergence D_KL(p‖q) is the expected number of extra bits incurred by coding samples from the true distribution p with a code optimal for q. It is nonnegative (Gibbs' inequality), zero iff p = q, but asymmetric and not a true metric. Mutual information is the special case D_KL(joint ‖ product of marginals), and cross-entropy = entropy + KL.
depths.deep: KL divergence is the natural 'distance' from a model to reality in information geometry, and minimizing it is exactly maximum-likelihood estimation — fitting a model to data minimizes D_KL(empirical ‖ model). Its asymmetry encodes a real modeling choice: D_KL(p‖q) penalizes q assigning low probability where p is high (mode-covering), while D_KL(q‖p) does the reverse (mode-seeking), a distinction that shapes variational inference and generative models.

atoms.note: Cross-entropy loss, ubiquitous in machine learning, is entropy plus KL divergence — minimizing it fits the model distribution to the data distribution.
sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
atoms.art_prompt: two distribution curves p and q with the shaded gap between them metered as wasted bits, an arrow noting the asymmetry p‖q ≠ q‖p

quiz.prompt: Why is KL divergence not a true distance metric?
quiz.answer: It is asymmetric (D_KL(p‖q) ≠ D_KL(q‖p)) and violates the triangle inequality, though it is nonnegative and zero iff p = q.

quiz.prompt: How is minimizing KL divergence related to maximum-likelihood estimation?
quiz.answer: Minimizing D_KL(empirical data ‖ model) over the model's parameters is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the data under the model.

atoms.title: Conditional probability and Bayes' rule
atoms.summary: Bayes' rule inverts conditional probabilities, updating a prior belief into a posterior in light of evidence.

depths.eli5: If you know how likely the evidence is when something is true, Bayes flips it to tell you how likely that something is now that you've seen the evidence.
depths.core: Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) is the probability of A given that B occurred. Bayes' rule rearranges this into P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), letting you invert a known likelihood P(B|A) into the desired posterior P(A|B) using the prior P(A). It is the engine of all probabilistic inference, from spam filters to medical diagnosis.
depths.deep: The base-rate fallacy is Bayes ignored: a rare condition (small prior) plus an imperfect test makes most positives false positives, no matter how 'accurate' the test sounds. Bayesian updating is also the discrete analogue of the maximum-entropy / inference view of statistical mechanics — both treat probability as a state of knowledge updated by constraints, not a property of the world alone.

atoms.note: P(B) in the denominator is the normalizer, expandable via the law of total probability: P(B) = Σ_A P(B|A)P(A).
sources: Wikipedia (facts): Bayes' theorem; Base rate fallacy
atoms.art_prompt: a prior bar being reshaped into a taller posterior bar by an arrow labeled with incoming evidence

quiz.prompt: A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000 people. Roughly, is a single positive result likely to be a true positive?
quiz.answer: No — with such a low base rate, false positives vastly outnumber true positives, so a lone positive is probably false (the base-rate fallacy).

quiz.prompt: In Bayes' rule, name the prior, likelihood, and posterior.
quiz.answer: Prior P(A), likelihood P(B|A), posterior P(A|B); P(B) is the normalizing evidence.

atoms.title: Regular expressions
atoms.summary: Regular expressions are an algebraic notation for patterns, exactly as expressive as finite automata.

depths.eli5: A regex is a compact pattern like 'one or more digits' that a machine can match against text. It describes the same patterns a simple state machine can recognize.
depths.core: Regular expressions build patterns from union (|), concatenation, and the Kleene star (zero-or-more repetition), starting from single symbols and the empty string. Kleene's theorem proves they describe exactly the regular languages — every regex compiles to an equivalent NFA, and every DFA converts back to a regex. They are the practical front-end to finite automata in text processing.
depths.deep: The Kleene star is what gives regular expressions unbounded length from a finite description, and it corresponds precisely to a loop (a revisited state) in the automaton. Real-world 'regex' engines often add backreferences, which push them beyond regular into a strictly more powerful (and worst-case exponential) regime — a frequent source of catastrophic-backtracking denial-of-service bugs.

atoms.art_prompt: a regex string compiling into an NFA diagram, with the Kleene star drawn as a loop back to an earlier state

quiz.prompt: What theorem equates regular expressions with finite automata?
quiz.answer: Kleene's theorem: regular expressions describe exactly the regular languages, equivalently those recognized by finite automata.

quiz.prompt: Why can a regex engine with backreferences behave worse than linear time?
quiz.answer: Backreferences exceed regular expressiveness, forcing backtracking search that can blow up exponentially — the catastrophic-backtracking ReDoS pitfall.

atoms.title: Greedy algorithms
atoms.summary: Greedy algorithms make the locally best choice at each step, which yields a global optimum only when the problem has matroid-like structure.

depths.eli5: Always grab the best-looking option right now and never look back. Sometimes that lands you the best overall answer; sometimes it traps you.
depths.core: A greedy algorithm builds a solution incrementally by taking the choice that looks best at each step. It is correct only when the problem has the greedy-choice property (a local optimum extends to a global one) and optimal substructure. Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal, Prim), Huffman coding, and interval scheduling are classic successes; the general 0/1 knapsack is a classic failure.
depths.deep: The deep reason greedy works for MST and not knapsack is matroid theory: greedy is provably optimal exactly on problems whose feasible sets form a matroid. When greedy fails, dynamic programming or exchange arguments are needed. Even when greedy is not optimal, it often gives a guaranteed approximation ratio, making it a workhorse for NP-hard problems.

sources: MIT OCW 6.046 Design and Analysis of Algorithms
atoms.art_prompt: a path picking the steepest immediate step each time, with one branch reaching the true summit and another stuck on a lower local peak

quiz.prompt: What property must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to be optimal?
quiz.answer: The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure — formally, the feasible structure forms a matroid.

quiz.prompt: Why does greedy fail for the 0/1 knapsack problem?
quiz.answer: Taking the highest value-per-weight item first can preclude a better combination; the locally best choice need not extend to a global optimum, so dynamic programming is required.

atoms.title: Amortized analysis
atoms.summary: Amortized analysis bounds the average cost per operation over a sequence, even when individual operations are occasionally expensive.

depths.eli5: Some operations are usually cheap but rarely costly. Amortized analysis spreads the rare big cost over the many cheap ones to find the true average.
depths.core: Amortized analysis measures the average cost of an operation across a worst-case sequence, not the worst single operation. A dynamic array that doubles when full costs O(n) on the resize but O(1) amortized per insertion, because resizes are rare. The aggregate, accounting (banker's), and potential methods are the three standard techniques for proving such bounds.
depths.deep: Amortized is not the same as average-case: it makes no probabilistic assumption, holding for every worst-case sequence. The potential method assigns the data structure a 'stored energy' Φ; the amortized cost is the actual cost plus ΔΦ, so cheap operations bank potential that expensive ones spend. This makes data structures like splay trees and Fibonacci heaps analyzable despite wild per-operation variance.

atoms.note: Amortized O(1) per op over n ops means total O(n) — distinct from, and stronger than, an average-case probabilistic claim.
sources: MIT OCW 6.046 Design and Analysis of Algorithms
atoms.art_prompt: a sequence of cheap insertions with an occasional tall resize bar, the tall cost averaged smoothly across the cheap ones

quiz.prompt: How does amortized analysis differ from average-case analysis?
quiz.answer: Amortized analysis averages over a worst-case sequence with no probabilistic assumptions; average-case assumes a distribution over inputs.

quiz.prompt: Why is insertion into a doubling dynamic array O(1) amortized despite O(n) resizes?
quiz.answer: Resizes happen only when the array is full and double its size, so the total resize work over n insertions is O(n), giving O(1) per insertion on average.

atoms.title: The time hierarchy theorem
atoms.summary: More time strictly buys more computational power: there are problems solvable in O(n^3) time but not in O(n^2).

depths.eli5: Give a computer genuinely more time and it can solve genuinely more problems. This is one of the few things about complexity we can actually prove.
depths.core: The time hierarchy theorem states that for time-constructible bounds with f growing sufficiently faster than g, DTIME(g) ⊊ DTIME(f): strictly more time yields strictly more decidable problems. The proof diagonalizes — it constructs a machine that, given more time, deliberately disagrees with every machine confined to less time. This is why P ⊊ EXP is a theorem, not a conjecture.
depths.deep: The hierarchy theorems are among the rare unconditional separations in complexity theory, and they work because diagonalization can be carried out within the time/space budget. Crucially, diagonalization alone cannot resolve P vs NP — relativization barriers (the Baker–Gill–Solovay result) show that any proof technique blind to machine internals fails on P vs NP, which is why that question remains open while hierarchy theorems are settled.

atoms.note: Hierarchy theorems give us our only proven separations (P ⊊ EXP, L ⊊ PSPACE); the famous open separations (P vs NP) provably need non-relativizing techniques.
sources: Wikipedia (facts): Time hierarchy theorem; Baker–Gill–Solovay theorem
atoms.art_prompt: nested time-budget rings, each strictly larger ring enclosing new problems unreachable by the inner ones, built by a diagonalizing machine

quiz.prompt: What does the time hierarchy theorem guarantee, and which separation does it prove?
quiz.answer: Sufficiently more time strictly increases solvable problems (DTIME(g) ⊊ DTIME(f)); it proves P ⊊ EXP.

quiz.prompt: Why can't the same diagonalization settle P vs NP?
quiz.answer: Diagonalization relativizes (works the same with any oracle), but Baker–Gill–Solovay built oracles making P vs NP go both ways, so relativizing techniques cannot resolve it.

atoms.title: Lossy compression and rate–distortion
atoms.equation: R(D)=\min_{p(\hat x\mid x):\,\mathbb{E}[d]\le D} I(X;\hat X)
atoms.summary: Rate–distortion theory gives the minimum number of bits needed to represent a source within an allowed level of distortion.

depths.eli5: If you're willing to lose a little quality, you can use far fewer bits. Rate–distortion tells you the best possible trade between size and fidelity.
depths.core: Lossless coding is bounded by entropy, but accepting some distortion D lets you compress further. The rate–distortion function R(D) is the minimum bit rate achievable while keeping the expected distortion below D, expressed as the minimum mutual information I(X;X̂) over reconstructions X̂ meeting the distortion constraint. It is the lossy counterpart to the source coding theorem and the theoretical floor for JPEG, MP3, and video codecs.
depths.deep: R(D) is convex and decreasing: R(0) recovers the entropy (lossless), and R grows steeply as you demand near-perfect fidelity. The curve formalizes the universal engineering trade-off between file size and quality. Rate–distortion is also the conceptual ancestor of the information bottleneck in deep learning, which compresses inputs while preserving information about a target — relevance-constrained lossy coding.

sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Rate–distortion theory; Information bottleneck method
atoms.art_prompt: a convex R(D) curve falling from the entropy at zero distortion, with codec quality knobs sliding along it trading size for fidelity

quiz.prompt: What does the rate–distortion function R(D) give, and what is R(0)?
quiz.answer: The minimum bit rate to represent a source within expected distortion D; R(0) equals the source entropy (lossless).

quiz.prompt: How does lossy compression beat the entropy bound?
quiz.answer: It does not reconstruct the source exactly — by tolerating bounded distortion it discards information the entropy bound assumed must be preserved, so fewer bits suffice.

atoms.title: Approximation algorithms
atoms.summary: When a problem is NP-hard, approximation algorithms find provably near-optimal solutions in polynomial time.

depths.eli5: If finding the perfect answer is too slow, settle for one guaranteed to be close — say, never worse than twice the best possible — but found quickly.
depths.core: An α-approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and always returns a solution within a factor α of optimal. For NP-hard optimization problems this is the practical response to intractability: vertex cover has a simple 2-approximation, set cover a (ln n)-approximation, and some problems admit a PTAS (approximation arbitrarily close to optimal). The achievable α is itself a deep question tied to hardness of approximation.
depths.deep: The PCP theorem reveals that for some problems even approximating is NP-hard: there is a threshold ratio below which no polynomial-time algorithm can go unless P = NP (e.g., MAX-3SAT is hard to approximate beyond 7/8). So NP-hardness comes in grades — some problems approximate arbitrarily well (PTAS), some to a fixed constant, and some not at all — refining the coarse P-vs-NP picture into a rich landscape of approximability.

atoms.note: Hardness of approximation (via the PCP theorem) shows some problems are not just hard to solve exactly but provably hard to even approximate beyond a fixed ratio.
sources: MIT OCW 6.046 Design and Analysis of Algorithms
atoms.art_prompt: an optimal solution bar beside a quickly-found approximate bar, with a guaranteed-ratio bracket showing the approximate is within factor α

quiz.prompt: What does it mean for an algorithm to be an α-approximation?
quiz.answer: It runs in polynomial time and always returns a solution within a factor α of the optimal value.

quiz.prompt: What does the PCP theorem imply about approximation?
quiz.answer: For some NP-hard problems, even approximating beyond a fixed ratio is itself NP-hard, so they cannot be approximated arbitrarily well unless P = NP.

atoms.title: Typical sequences and the AEP
atoms.summary: For long sequences of i.i.d. symbols, almost all probability concentrates on roughly 2^{nH} nearly-equiprobable 'typical' sequences.

depths.eli5: If you flip a biased coin a million times, the result you get is almost certainly one of a predictable family of outcomes — the 'typical' ones — and there are about 2 to the power (length times entropy) of them.
depths.core: The asymptotic equipartition property (AEP) is the information-theoretic law of large numbers: as n grows, the per-symbol log-probability of an i.i.d. sequence converges to the entropy H(X). Consequently the probability mass concentrates on a typical set of about 2^{nH} sequences, each with probability near 2^{-nH}. This is the precise reason H bits per symbol suffice for compression — you only need to index the typical set.
depths.deep: The AEP is what makes Shannon's source and channel coding theorems provable: compression assigns short codes only to typical sequences (ignoring the vanishingly rare atypical ones), and channel coding picks codewords so their typical outputs barely overlap. The exponential gap between the 2^{nH} typical sequences and the |alphabet|^n total sequences is the quantitative heart of why information can be compressed at all.

atoms.note: Typical set size ≈ 2^{nH}; total sequence count = |X|^n. Compression works because the typical set is exponentially smaller whenever H < log|X|.
sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Asymptotic equipartition property; Typical set

quiz.prompt: Approximately how many typical sequences are there for n i.i.d. symbols with entropy H, and what is each one's probability?
quiz.answer: About 2^{nH} typical sequences, each with probability roughly 2^{-nH}.

quiz.prompt: How does the AEP justify compressing a source to H bits per symbol?
quiz.answer: Almost all probability sits on the ~2^{nH} typical sequences, so you only need ~nH bits to index them, ignoring the vanishingly rare rest — matching the entropy bound.
